newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl's party chiefs approve tax cutting plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl's party chiefs approve tax cutting plan.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrat (CDU) party executive gave its overwhelming approval on Monday to a tax-cutting plan intended to reduce the overall burden on German taxpayers by 30 billion marks ($19.6 billion) from 1999.

Party bosses unanimously backed an amended plan drafted by Kohl's parliamentary party chief Wolfgang Schaeuble to simplify and make fairer Germany's complex tax system, general secretary Peter Hintze told a news conference.
The main plank of the Schaeuble plan, which will go before the annual CDU party conference later this month, is to slash the top rate of income tax to 35 percent from 53 percent now.
The entry rate would fall to around 20 percent from 26 percent, while the cuts would be offset in part by scrapping a series of tax breaks.
But the CDU resisted pressure from junior coalition partner the Free Democrats (FDP) and from opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to bring in the reforms earlier.
"I can clearly state that the date of January 1, 1999 remains," Hintze said. "The technically clean preparation of this "reform of the century' will take time."
Two changes were inserted into the tax plan.
A tougher capital gains tax would take account of losses as well as profits in real estate and securities dealings after 1999. The original draft had only considered profits.
The draft also leaves open the possibility to exempt some social security payments like unemployment benefit and sick pay from income tax assessments.
While the approval of his tax plan gives the influential Schaeuble a boost, a lot of haggling among Germany's political parties can be expected before it takes proper shape.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, leader of the Bavarian CDU sister-party the Christian Social Union (CSU), has given only guarded support. He did not sit in on the CDU meeting.
With the 15 billion mark privatisation of Deutsche Telekom AG -- Europe's biggest ever -- entering its final phase, Waigel is wary of scaring off investors.

He said after a CSU party meeting in Munich that he would not endorse the capital gains proposal until it had been reviewed by tax experts. But he said he feared it could push trade away from Germany into foreign financial markets.

The CDU plan would tax capital gains on all sales of securities or real estate, not just speculative sales of assets held less than six months, the current German practice. Capital gains on sales of people's main homes would be exempted.
The SPD, which controls the Bundesrat upper house of parliament and can block government tax measures there, again called on Monday for the reform to take effect in 1998.

SPD head Oskar Lafontaine, speaking after a party gathering in Berlin, said he was open to discuss income tax rate cuts. But he opposed any offsetting increases in value-added tax, as had been suggested in the past by Kohl.
SPD regional leaders are locked in talks with Waigel over finding a compromise to the 1997 tax bill -- recently blocked in the Bundesrat -- and the two sides were due to meet again on Monday evening.

Waigel called for the SPD to show more readiness to compromise in talks on the bill -- part of a 70 billion mark austerity plan intended to make Germany qualify next year for the planned launch of the single European currency in 1999.
